name: Cumbia Clasica
desc: Classic Colombian cumbia: tambora marks the duple pulse while the llamador locks the steady offbeat (upbeat) accents that drive the dance. Maracas/guacharaca keep the continuous eighth texture.

name: Cumbia Tambor Alegre
desc: Syncopated improvising part of the tambor alegre over the cumbia base, emphasizing offbeats and pushing into the upbeats. The deep tambora anchors beats one and three.

name: Cumbia Drumset Adaptation
desc: Modern kit translation of traditional cumbia, with the bass tracing the tambora and the rim/snare echoing the alegre accents. Common in Colombian and Panamanian dance bands.

name: Porro Sabanero
desc: Festive brass-band porro from the Sinu and savanna region, blending gaita drumming with European bombo and platillo. The bombo strikes on the beat while the redoblante answers on the offbeats.

name: Gaita Larga
desc: Cane-flute gaita ensemble with interlocking tambora, alegre and llamador under the gaita hembra melody. The llamador holds the offbeat while the tambora drives the duple base.

name: Bullerengue Sentao
desc: Medium-tempo Afro-Colombian bullerengue led by elder women with handclaps and call-and-response; the alegre syncopates over the llamador offbeat and tambora pulse.

name: Bullerengue Chalupa
desc: Fast chalupa variant of bullerengue with dense alegre improvisation and rapid clapping. The driving tambora marks every beat under busy offbeat accents.

name: Mapale
desc: Frenetic Afro-Colombian mapale with relentless drumming and frantic dance; the tambora hammers the beats while the alegre packs the offbeats with rapid accents and clapping.

name: Currulao
desc: Afro-Pacific marimba currulao in lilting 6/8 with interlocking cununos and bombos; the bombo golpeador marks the cycle while the bombo arrullador and guasa hold the ternary texture.

name: Currulao Bambuco Viejo
desc: Bambuco viejo currulao variant where the cununo macho drives steady ternary figures and the cununo hembra replies with offbeat fills over the bombo's deep pulses.

name: Champeta Criolla
desc: Cartagena champeta (terapia) built on a syncopated electronic bassline and conga groove rooted in Congolese soukous. Snare/clap lands on the backbeat with offbeat hat accents.

name: Vallenato Paseo
desc: Most-recorded vallenato air, the cheerful paseo in 2/4 with the caja marking accents and the guacharaca scraping its quarter-plus-two-eighths down-down-up pattern.

name: Vallenato Son
desc: Slowest, most delicate vallenato air in 2/4, used for laments; the caja keeps a breath-like steady accompaniment under the accordion's bass-button melody.

name: Vallenato Merengue
desc: Merengue vallenato in lively 6/8 with a regular two-feel and strong Spanish influence; the caja and guacharaca outline the ternary swing under the accordion.

name: Vallenato Puya
desc: Fastest vallenato air in 6/8, opening like the merengue then breaking into the rapid improvised cierre where caja, guacharaca and accordion trade solos.

name: Chande
desc: Coastal chande, a flute-and-drum costeno form related to cumbia and tambora; the llamador holds the offbeat while the tambora drives the carnival pulse.

name: Fandango de Bullerengue
desc: Caribbean Colombian fandango with fast jumps; the tambora emphasizes the llamador accents and adds stick strokes on the drum shell, blending African, Indigenous and Spanish rhythm.

name: Bambuco
desc: National Andean Colombian song-dance in lilting 6/8 with constant sesquialtera (3/4 against 6/8); tiple and guitar carry the bi-metric strum and syncopated pulse.

name: Pasillo Fiestero
desc: Fast, lively party pasillo from the Andean region, a fiesta variant felt in a brisk waltz-derived 3/4; tiple and guitar drive the danceable couple movement.

name: Joropo Llanero Corrido
desc: Joropo llanero por corrido with harp, cuatro and maracas in classic sesquialtera, alternating 6/8 and 3/4; the maracas roll continuous cross-rhythms supporting the cuatro accents.

name: Joropo Llanero Por Derecho
desc: Joropo por derecho where the harp bordones drive the 3/4 against the 6/8 treble, producing the vertical sesquialtera; maracas and cuatro lock the hemiola.

name: Joropo Central Tuyero
desc: Joropo central (tuyero) from the Venezuelan central coast, built on harp and buche with maracas; the 3-against-2 sesquialtera defines the swaying ternary groove.

name: Golpe Larense
desc: Golpe from the Lara region, a joropo cousin in 6/8 hemiola played on cuatro, cinco and tambora; the strummed accents outline the sesquialtera under improvised verses.

name: Tambor Culo'e Puya
desc: Barlovento culo'e puya, three tall redondo drums interlocking for the San Juan Bautista festival; the prima and cruzao weave fast figures over the pujao's base pulse.

name: Tambor Sangueo
desc: Slow, ceremonial sangueo golpe played on mina and curbata to process the image of San Juan; the deep two-measure cycle drives the procession through the town.

name: Tambor Mina y Curbata
desc: Tambor mina ensemble from the central coast, the long mina struck with sticks while the curbata answers and laures strike the body; an Afro-Venezuelan festival groove.

name: Gaita Zuliana
desc: Festive Zulian Christmas gaita in 6/8 accenting beats 1 and 4; the furro drones the bass, tambora hits accents and fills, charrasca and maracas keep the ternary texture.

name: Merengue Caraqueno
desc: Venezuelan merengue rucaneao in its signature irregular 5/8 subdivided 3+2; the asymmetric accent pattern gives the Caracas dance its distinctive limping swing.

name: Calipso de El Callao
desc: Carnival calypso from the mining town of El Callao in Guayana, a 4/4 syncopated groove on the open-ended bumbac drum with rallo, campana and steel pans.

name: Son Jarocho Golpe
desc: Veracruz son jarocho in 6/8 where the golpe accent pattern falls on the first, fourth and sixth pulses, articulated by jarana downstrokes and the tarima zapateado.

name: Son Jarocho Zapateado
desc: Dense zapateado footwork over the jarocho sesquialtera; dancers on the tarima act as a percussion instrument, the heelwork tracing both the 6/8 and 3/4 feels.

name: Son Huasteco Huapango
desc: Huapango from the Huasteca, a 6/8 son with marked sesquialtera and falsetto vocals; jarana and huapanguera strum the cross-rhythm while violin improvises.

name: Son Jalisciense
desc: Mariachi son jalisciense felt in 12/8 with sesquialtera and contratiempos; vihuela and guitarron drive the manico while harp and violins trade phrases.

name: Mariachi Huapango
desc: Mariachi huapango alternating a measure of 6/8 with a measure of 3/4 (sesquialtera); the vihuela manico and guitarron outline the shifting accent against the violins.

name: Danzon Baqueteo
desc: Danzon baqueteo on timbales, a composite of cinquillo and tresillo in 2/4 popularized in Veracruz; guiro and claves maintain the syncopation under the charanga.

name: Danzon Cinquillo
desc: The cinquillo cell (eighth-sixteenth-eighth-sixteenth-eighth) underpinning danzon, the first written music organized by Afro-Cuban clave, strongly syncopated in 2/4.

name: Banda Tambora
desc: Sinaloan banda oom-pah, the tambora (bass drum) on the downbeats and tarola (snare) on the offbeats, the tuba doubling the bass under massed brass.

name: Banda Tambora Quebradita
desc: Up-tempo quebradita banda groove, the tuba pumping the bass on the beats while the tarola cracks the offbeats and the tambora drives the dancehall feel.

name: Norteno Polka
desc: Classic norteno polka in crisp 2/4 with the bajo sexto thumping bass on beat one and the chordal offbeat on beat two, the accordion carrying the melody.

name: Norteno Redova
desc: Norteno redova, a triple-meter dance form adapted from European immigrants, with the bajo sexto bass on the downbeat and chordal answers on the upper beats.

name: Norteno Vals
desc: Norteno vals (waltz), bass on beat one with two chordal afterbeats; one of the European dance meters the accordion-bajo sexto duo adapted in northern Mexico.

name: Cumbia Sonidera
desc: Mexico City and Puebla sound-system cumbia at 90-105 BPM, kick on the strong beats, clap/snare on the backbeat, guiro and timbales articulating syncopations.

name: Cumbia Rebajada
desc: Monterrey cumbia rebajada, the classic cumbia groove slowed to roughly 76 BPM for a heavy, syrupy, head-nodding swing tied to cholombiano sonidero culture.

name: Chilena de la Costa
desc: Chilena from the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca, a cueca-derived son in bright 6/8 sesquialtera with handkerchief dancing, gritos and buoyant zapateado.

name: Tamborito Panameno
desc: Panama's national tamborito with cantadora and female chorus over a three-drum battery; the pujador keeps time, the repicador improvises, the caja anchors the bass amid handclaps.

name: Tamborito Repicador
desc: Improvisatory high repicador layer of the tamborito, answering the singer and chorus with rapid figures over the pujador's steady palm strokes and the caja bass.

name: Cumbia Panamena
desc: Panamanian cumbia from the Azuero region with accordion, tambores and churuca; the caja and pujador hold the offbeat while the bass drum drives the duple base.

name: Mejorana
desc: Mejorana from the Azuero Peninsula, a zapateo-derived dance accompanied by the five-string mejoranera over improvised decimas in a swaying ternary feel.

name: Son Chapin
desc: Guatemala's national son chapin played on marimba with 3:2 sesquialtera; ornate right-hand figures over a steady bass ostinato accompany the zapateado couple-dance.

name: Marimba Son Guatemalteco
desc: Guatemalan marimba ensemble son with hemiola cross-rhythm and chorused tremolo; guitars, guitarrilla and maracas reinforce the 6/8 against 3/4 swing.

name: Marimba Son Chiapaneco
desc: Marimba son of the Chiapas and Central American highlands, the bass marking the ternary beats while treble mallets trace the sesquialtera over a singing tremolo.

name: Palo de Mayo
desc: Afro-Nicaraguan maypole music from Bluefields, an electrified, up-tempo mento built on heavy drums, calypso and soca, with backbeat snare and syncopated bass.

name: Marimba Son Costarricense
desc: Guanacaste marimba son from Costa Rica in 6/8 sesquialtera, the diatonic marimba accompanying the punto guanacasteco couple-dance with handkerchiefs and bombas.
